prediction:
THOUGHT: This 18-month-old female presents with a constellation of concerning findings: precocious vaginal bleeding (brown discharge with clots), bilateral breast enlargement (thelarche), multiple café-au-lait spots, limping, left leg bone pain since a fall 2 months ago, and tenderness on palpation of the left lower leg. Physical exam reveals no genital trauma, intact hymen, and normal external genitalia — making abuse or local trauma unlikely as cause of bleeding. The presence of café-au-lait macules (>2–3 cm, multiple) strongly suggests an underlying genetic syndrome. The radiograph shows patchy lytic and sclerotic changes in the femoral metaphysis — highly suggestive of a bone lesion, not a simple fracture (which would have healed by 2 months). This pattern is classic for fibrous dysplasia (FD), especially when associated with café-au-lait spots and endocrine abnormalities (e.g., precocious puberty). In girls, McCune-Albright Syndrome (MAS) is characterized by the triad of: (1) polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, (2) café-au-lait skin pigmentation (often with “coast of Maine” borders), and (3) autonomous endocrine hyperfunction — most commonly gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty (due to ovarian cysts/estrogen excess), presenting with vaginal bleeding and breast development before age 3. The absence of pubic hair (adrenarche) and normal electrolytes argue against congenital adrenal hyperplasia or other adrenal causes. CBC is normal, ruling out leukemia or marrow infiltration as cause of bone pain/bleeding. The bone pain and limping are consistent with active or expanding fibrous dysplasia lesion(s); the femoral metaphysis is a common site. The vaginal bleeding is estrogen-driven from autonomous ovarian activation — a hallmark of MAS. No evidence of coagulopathy (no bruising, nosebleeds, normal platelets), and hymenal integrity makes sexual abuse highly unlikely.

DIAGNOSIS: McCune-Albright Syndrome
